item.title: Is It Wrong to Laugh at Your Partner's Misfortune?
item.description:
Relationships

Is It Wrong to Laugh at Your Partner's Misfortune?

Why laughing at harmless mistakes can deepen intimacy.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • Laughing at a partner's harmless overconfidence can reinforce relational equality.
  • Not all schadenfreude is malicious; context determines its moral significance.
  • Benign schadenfreude involves deservingness, mild setbacks, and passive observation
  • Secure romantic love allows room for humor, playfulness, and human imperfection.

"The misfortune of others tastes like honey." — Japanese proverb

Your partner insists they never make mistakes. Minutes later, they confidently walk into a glass door or discover they parked on the wrong street. You cannot help smiling. Does that make you a bad partner—or could it actually reveal something healthy about your relationship?

Love is usually associated with celebrating a partner's successes and easing their suffering. Yet many loving couples occasionally laugh at one another's harmless blunders. This apparent contradiction points to a neglected psychological phenomenon. Although schadenfreude literally means "joy at another's harm," not every form of schadenfreude is malicious. In romantic relationships, a mild version may reflect affection, equality, and emotional security rather than hostility. This benign form does not weaken romantic love; under the right conditions, it may actually reinforce it by normalizing imperfection and restoring interpersonal balance.

The Bad Reputation of Schadenfreude

"It is not enough to succeed; others must fail." — Gore Vidal

Schadenfreude has long been regarded as one of our darker emotions. Schopenhauer (1840) described it as among the worst traits in human nature because of its close association with cruelty. More recently, Ortony and colleagues (2022) argued that schadenfreude generally reflects "pure ill will," while others suggest that it can even involve dehumanizing its target (Wang et al., 2019).

There is good reason for this negative reputation. When people seek another person's suffering or delight in serious misfortune, schadenfreude is indeed malicious. Yet this traditional view overlooks a milder form that permeates everyday social life. Schadenfreude exists on a continuum, ranging from cruel delight in another's pain to gentle amusement at a minor setback. The benign form involves taking pleasure in a small, often deserved mishap without wishing genuine harm on the other person.

Defining schadenfreude merely as pleasure at another's misfortune obscures its psychological complexity. The moral meaning of schadenfreude depends not merely on the pleasure itself, but also on why it occurs, how serious the misfortune is, and what relationship exists between the people involved.

What Makes Schadenfreude Benign?

The phrase "benign schadenfreude" may sound like a contradiction. Yet much of everyday humor rests precisely on our ability to laugh at harmless human foibles without wishing genuine harm on anyone. Three characteristics distinguish benign schadenfreude: deservingness, limited severity, and passivity (Ben-Ze'ev, 2000, 2014; Van Dijk & Ouwerkerk, 2014).

Deservingness

A central feature of schadenfreude is the belief that the other person deserves what happened. This concern with deservingness also lies at the heart of emotions such as envy and jealousy.

Imagine sitting in heavy traffic while another driver speeds illegally along the shoulder. Moments later, a police officer pulls the driver over. Irritation often turns into satisfaction—not because we enjoy another person's suffering, but because justice appears to have been restored. Although judgments of deservingness are often subjective, people commonly agree when someone has brought a minor setback upon themselves.

Moderate misfortune

A second defining characteristic is that the misfortune is relatively minor. Suppose an arrogant and inconsiderate neighbor discovers that his new car has been scratched. We may experience a fleeting sense of satisfaction. But if his daughter develops a serious illness, that satisfaction almost certainly disappears, replaced by sympathy and compassion. Severe suffering typically overrides any pleasure one might otherwise feel. Benign schadenfreude therefore thrives when the setback bruises the ego rather than devastates the person. Like many emotions, it is sensitive to proportion.

Passivity

A third defining feature is passivity. The observer enjoys witnessing an event rather than causing it. This distinction is morally significant. Even when we believe someone deserves punishment, we generally lack the authority to impose it ourselves. Creating another person's misfortune transforms detached amusement into genuine moral wrongdoing (Barron et al., 2023).

These three characteristics distinguish benign from malicious schadenfreude. In sadism—the extreme form of malicious schadenfreude—the opposite pattern emerges: the victim need not deserve the suffering, the harm is often severe, and the observer actively seeks it. Cruelty is central to sadism but absent from benign schadenfreude.

Schadenfreude in Romantic Relationships

"Angels fly because they take themselves lightly." — G. K. Chesterton

At first glance, romantic love appears incompatible with schadenfreude. Love encourages us to celebrate our partner's achievements, whereas schadenfreude involves pleasure at another person's setback. Yet benign schadenfreude is surprisingly common in flourishing relationships.

The paradox disappears once we recognize that profound love does not require idealizing one's partner. On the contrary, healthy love allows partners to acknowledge each other's imperfections without threatening the relationship itself. Malicious schadenfreude has no place in profound romantic love. The benign form, however, often emerges in relationships characterized by trust, affection, and emotional security. Rather than expressing superiority, it often reflects confidence that the relationship is strong enough to withstand playful teasing.

Humor is valued both in choosing romantic partners and in sustaining long-term relationships. A good sense of humor may signal psychological flexibility, creativity, and social intelligence—all qualities that facilitate successful partnerships. Humor also helps partners regulate conflict, reduce tension, and recover more quickly from everyday frustrations. More broadly, playfulness promotes intimacy, strengthens emotional bonds, and helps couples navigate life's inevitable frustrations (Hall & France, 2024; Langley & Shiota, 2025).

A benign form of schadenfreude adds another layer to this playfulness. It gently punctures excessive pride, reminds partners of their shared human fallibility, and subtly restores equality when one person has become overly self-assured. When one partner becomes temporarily self-important, a harmless mishap can gently restore symmetry, reminding both partners that intimacy flourishes between equals rather than idols. Laughing when your partner's overconfidence is punctured by a harmless mistake need not signal hostility. Instead, it may express the comfort of balance while knowing that neither partner must appear flawless in order to remain deeply loved.

This form of amusement is therefore most likely to flourish in relationships grounded in mutual goodwill. Partners secure in each other's love can tease, laugh, and occasionally enjoy each other's small embarrassments without questioning the relationship itself. Indeed, one of the clearest signs of relational security is the ability of both partners to laugh—not only at each other, but also at themselves. Couples who can smile together at life's small absurdities often possess the resilience to withstand its larger challenges.

The Bottom Line

Healthy love is not humorless admiration. It is secure enough to accommodate imperfection.

There is an important difference between laughing at your partner and laughing with your partner. In healthy relationships, an initial laugh at a harmless mishap often turns into shared laughter, making the experience fundamentally relational rather than adversarial.

Occasionally smiling at a partner's minor, self-inflicted setback need not diminish love. When rooted in affection, proportionality, and mutual respect, such amusement can reflect something surprisingly positive: a relationship that is secure enough to acknowledge human imperfections without diminishing mutual regard. Ultimately, benign schadenfreude reminds us that neither partner is above the other and neither must be perfect to be deeply loved. When love is secure, even life's small misfortunes can become moments of shared sweetness rather than shared pain.

item.title: On Screen: Why We Cheat
item.description:
Infidelity

On Screen: Why We Cheat

5 films across genres reveal different reasons for betrayal.

Posted July 25, 2026

Key points
  • According to a 2012 study, nearly one in three men and one in five women report having had extramarital sex.
  • Infidelity often stems from unmet needs or emotional disconnection, not love for someone new.
  • An affair can push couples toward honesty that deepens desire and intimacy.

Five of the most hurtful events in our intimate relationships are criticism, active disassociation, passive disassociation, infidelity, and deception. Infidelity, in particular, can create intense emotional distress, including depression, anxiety, loss of self-esteem, and trauma. Infidelity is essentially a behavior by one partner that breaks a contract that two people have with each other.

In a large study conducted by Elizabeth S. Allen and David C. Atkins in the Journal of Family Issues in 2012, they found, with large representative samples, that 34 percent of men and 19 percent of women had extramarital sex at some point, and within that sample, they acknowledged that it is probably slightly underreported and that the statistics do not include emotional affairs, which can be just as hurtful.

After an affair is disclosed to a partner, couples can experience a wave of emotional reactions from intense anger and betrayal to chaos and confusion to acceptance and grief. One of the most painful questions that individuals can ruminate over is, “Why did they cheat?” There are many reasons and theories as to why individuals cheat, such as attachment issues, personality traits of the cheater, or a societal adaptation for unmet needs.

Despite how upsetting and destructive infidelity is, relationship therapist Esther Perel reminds us that affairs can also reshape our relationships by revealing those unfulfilled needs and can create new conversations that bring more desire and intimacy into the relationship.

The five films below explore some common reasons for betrayal.

"The Ice Storm"
Source: Fox Searchlight Pictures

The Ice Storm (1997): Ang Lee brilliantly captures 1970s suburban life in this drama based on Rick Moody's novel. Two Connecticut families (starring Sigourney Weaver and Kevin Kline) approach affairs more as an existential crisis than out of love or even desire. The cheating is more about dissociation and numbing out, as a chilly, metaphorical ice storm covers the neighborhood. Their affairs turn out to be a destructive and devastating escape from emotional disconnection.

"Unfaithful"
Source: 20th Century Fox

Unfaithful (2002): In this thriller, Connie Sumner (Diane Lane) seeks aliveness, thrill, and excitement in her relatively stable 11-year marriage with Edward (Richard Gere). Her affair is impulsive, and she immediately regrets it afterward. However, her marriage no longer gives her the dopamine and adrenaline rush that the young, handsome bookseller Paul (Olivier Martinez) does. Connie chases desire, but the thrill comes at a serious cost to her home life. Connie begins to spiral into jealousy, rage, guilt, and eventually violence.

"Closer"
Source: Columbia Pictures

Closer (2004): Adapted from Patrick Marber's play, this film can be divisive for the audience because it peels back every layer of the onion, so to speak. Dan (Jude Law), who seems to only want what is always out of reach instead of what he has, and Anna (Julia Roberts), who has unresolved feelings for Dan, have an affair that sets off an entire cycle of intense emotional reactions for them and those they betray (Natalie Portman and Clive Owen). Instead of moving forward, each partner tries to pick apart every tiny detail on when, where, why, how, and what so that repair seems impossible.

"Crazy Stupid Love"
Source: Warner Bros. Pictures

Crazy Stupid Love (2011): In this romantic comedy, the affair is not so much a destroyer as an awakener. Emily (Julianne Moore) cheats on her husband, Cal (Steve Carell), because her needs have gone unmet for so long. After dating and rediscovering, with the help of Jacob (Ryan Gosling), who he is, Cal realizes he took Emily for granted for years in their marriage. Unlike the other films, this one ends with Cal and Emily reconciling.

"The Other Woman"
Source: 20th Century Fox

The Other Woman (2014): In this hilarious comedy, the husband (Nikolaj Coster-Waldau) is a serial cheater and womanizer. He has narcissistic personality traits and uses gaslighting and lying to cover his actions. He has multiple girlfriends, but what is so fun (and funny) about this film is that two of his mistresses (Cameron Diaz and Kate Upton) and his wife (Leslie Mann) team up, turn their grief into action, and focus on repairing by moving on in female solidarity.
